units.translation: 1212-14a. Until the Bacchiadae: Bacchis was a son of Dionysus, and he spent time in Corinth. Those descended from him were most noble, and they came to Epirus and settled around the Ceraunian mountains. They also founded Euboea (with Abas leading, as Kaibel supplements), whence they were called Abantes and, by a change of letters, Amantes (Orus). Stephanus of Byzantium, 'Abantis': Euboea ... the feminine Abantia, which by a barbarian change of b to m was called Amantia in Antigonus' Macedonian Periegesis (fr. 3 M. IV 306). Callimachus called it Amantinē (Xylander; manuscripts have mant-) like Leontinē (see above): 'and they settled Amantinē Orician' (Holstenius; manuscripts have -ēsan). The same author, 'Amantia': a part of the Illyrians near Oricus and Corcyra, settled by Abantes who returned from Troy. Callimachus calls it Amantinē. ... They are also called Amantes (Meineke; manuscripts have Ab-). ... and they say Abantes themselves. Cf. W 94, scholium on Lycophron 1042, Tzetzes on the same, Hesychius 'Amantoi'.

who were expelled from Corinth because of the death of Actaeon. The reason is this: Melissus, having benefited the Corinthians—for when they were about to be destroyed by Pheidon, king of the Argives, he rescued them—was deemed worthy of honor by them. 〈...〉 And then the Bacchiadae, coming by night to the house of Actaeon, wanted to drag away the boy; but when his parents resisted, it happened that Actaeon was torn apart. When the Isthmian games were about to be held, Melissus stood upon the altar and called down many curses upon the Corinthians if they did not avenge the death of his son; having said this, he threw himself down the cliff below. The Corinthians, being careful not to leave the death of Actaeon unavenged, and at the same time the god commanding it, expelled the Bacchiadae. Chersicrates, one of the Bacchiadae, founded Corcyra, driving out the Colchians who inhabited it; but they, being expelled, went to Epirus.

b. From Ephyra: Ephyra is Corinth, named after Ephyra, daughter of Epimetheus; but Eumelus (fr. 1 Kinkel 187) says it is from Ephyra, daughter of Oceanus and Tethys, who became the wife of Epimetheus.

1215. And the Nestaeans: Scylax (Periplus of the Inner Sea, fr. 4, Geographi Graeci Minores I, XXXV) says the Nestaeans are an Illyrian people; from them there is a coastal voyage into the gulf 〈...〉. And Eratosthenes in the third book of his Geography says (fr. III B 112 Berger): 'After the Illyrians come the Nestaeans, off whom is the island Pharos, a colony of the Parians.'
1216. But these things while he was going: meaning 'after a long time'.
